newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila and his rebels proclaim victory in Zaire. [CORRECTED 09:42 GMT 18/5]
newsitem.headline: Kabila and his rebels proclaim victory in Zaire. [CORRECTED 09:42 GMT 18/5]

text.p: Laurent Kabila and his rebels proclaimed victory in Zaire's seven-month civil war and purged Africa's third largest nation of one of the more obvious symbols of ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko's rule -- its name.

Kabila, 56, declared himself head of state in a statement which he read at his headquarters in the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi on Saturday as his forces moved into Kinshasa virtually unopposed to the cheers of jubilant residents.

"Mr Laurent Desire Kabila assumes from today the functions of the head of state of the Democratic Republic of the Congo," it said, reverting to the name Zaire had from 1964 until Mobutu changed it in 1971 (corrects from "...the name Zaire had on independence from Belgium in 1960 until Mobutu changed it in 1971").

But sporadic exchanges of mortar and automatic weapons fire were heard nightfall in Kinshasa and reports of shoot-outs with die-hard Mobutu loyalists suggested that the rebels still had to consolidate their hold over the city of five million people.

Across the river in Brazzaville, capital of Congo, members of Mobutu's close family gathered for a plane flight into exile. Mobutu was reported to be in his jungle palace at his ancestral home of Gbadolite.
Officials in Morocco said Mobutu, who has cancer, and his family were expected there.

In its first broadcast over national radio in Kinshasa, the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire ordered all government troops to report by Sunday morning and warned looters they would be severely punished.
Kabila, whose revolt mushroomed from an October dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, said he would set up a transitional government of public salvation within 72 hours.

He also pledged a constituent assembly within 60 days to work out a new transitional constitution, to replace the one agreed after a reluctant Mobutu bowed to foreign and domestic pressure for multi-party politics in 1990.
The United States, former colonial power Belgium, France, one of Mobutu's last friends, and Germany reacted to Kabila's victory by calling for a broad-based government and elections.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, speaking in Moscow, had a similar message for Kabila, urging him to respect the "choice and the voice" of the Zairean people.
Mobutu, 66, seized power in 1965 and proved one of Africa's most enduring strongmen. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.

Critics denounced him as everything from a dictator to a thief and accused him of plundering what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries and amassing a huge personal fortune while his people struggled against poverty and neglect.

Characteristically defiant, Mobutu refused to resign as head of state, as demanded by Kabila, but his abrupt departure from the capital on Friday triggered intense speculation that he was on his way to exile.

One airport official in Brazzaville said the presidential plane collecting Mobutu's soldier son Kongolo and the commander of his feared presidential guard, General Nzimbi Ngbale, might stop at Gbadolite to pick up the veteran leader.

Moroccan officials said Mobutu was expected to spend time there but Switzerland, sensitive to accusations that it handled dirty money, froze all the Mobutu family assets in its banks and on its territory.

Initial reports on casualties in Kinshasa as the rebels moved in were sketchy, but defence minister and army chief of staff General Mahele Lieko Bokungo was killed on Friday night by members of the presidential guard.
Diplomats said Mahele had been planning to meet Kabila to discuss handing over power.
